title: Ninety minutes to put it back
where: ESM, Kirchberg — IT & Digital, the operations room behind the third-floor server suite

lines.text: The operations room has no windows and one clock four minutes fast, which everybody in it has agreed not to fix. Two screens, a printed runbook, and a duty manager who has blocked out the whole afternoon.
lines.plain: The operations room has no windows. It has one clock that is four minutes fast, and everybody has agreed not to fix it. There are two screens, a printed runbook, and a duty manager who has kept the whole afternoon free.

lines.text: The last dry-run before Release 3. The Release 1 cut-over in March overran by forty minutes on the configuration step, and the plan has had a revision history ever since, like a piece of code.
lines.plain: This is the last practice run before Release 3. The Release 1 cut-over in March took forty minutes longer than planned, because of the configuration step. Since then the plan has had a revision history, like software.
g: cut-over
the planned switch from the old way of working to the new system, at a fixed time
ref: Assure the Operations team can understand the Deployment Plan and successfully deploy, operate and manage the solution in a pre-production environment

lines.text: Before anyone opens anything. On the first of February my duty manager owns this at three in the morning and she has never met Charles. Read it to me as if I were her.
lines.plain: Before anyone opens anything, I want one thing clear. From 1 February my duty manager owns this system at three in the morning, and she has never met Charles. Read the plan to me as if I were her.

lines.text: Four units in September. Data layer, reconciliation API, portal, and the external gateway, which is new and is why we are in this room three weeks early instead of one.
lines.plain: In September there are four deployment units: the data layer, the reconciliation API, the portal, and the external access gateway. The gateway is new. That is why we are testing three weeks early instead of one.

lines.text: Portal and API are blue-green. Two of everything, cut the traffic over, cut it back in ninety seconds if it screams. The data layer is not blue-green and never will be. A replica reload is ninety minutes.
lines.plain: The portal and the API use two parallel environments. We switch traffic to the new one, and we can switch it back in ninety seconds if there is a problem. The data layer does not work that way and never will. Reloading the replica takes ninety minutes.

lines.text: So my back-out is ninety minutes, not ninety seconds.
lines.plain: So putting the old version back takes ninety minutes, not ninety seconds.
g: back-out procedure
the agreed steps for putting the old version back if a deployment goes wrong

lines.text: Ninety minutes, and the decision is at twenty-two hundred. Not twenty-two thirty while somebody has one more idea. Twenty-two hundred, one name, and the name is the duty manager's, not mine.
lines.plain: Ninety minutes, and the decision is made at 22:00. Not at 22:30, while somebody tries one more idea. At 22:00, by one named person, and that person is the duty manager, not me.
ref: it is closely related to IT operations such as cut-over, rollbacks, back-out procedures for contingency and risk management

lines.text: And nothing the gateway does is visible on the twenty-sixth. It deploys dark. What ships that evening and what opens on the twenty-seventh are two different events, and only the first one is yours.
lines.plain: Also, nothing the gateway does will be visible on 26 September. It is deployed but switched off. What is installed that evening and what is opened on 27 September are two different events. Only the first one belongs to operations.

lines.text: Good. I have deployed things at midnight that turned out to be policy decisions. Twice.
lines.plain: Good. Twice in my career I have installed something at midnight and discovered it was really a policy decision.

lines.text: How does it get validated? Not by us saying it looks right.
lines.plain: How do we check the deployment worked? Not by us saying it looks correct.

lines.text: One member state's total against last night's reconciled control figure. Match to the cent or the deploy is a failure. And the script picks the member state, because if I fix it to Portugal somebody eventually makes Portugal work.
lines.plain: We compare one member state's total against last night's reconciled control figure. If it does not match exactly, the deployment has failed. The script chooses which member state, because if I always used Portugal, somebody would eventually make Portugal work and nothing else.
g: smoke test
a few quick checks after deployment to prove the system basically works
ref: Specific stress and performance tests, smoke tests with some key features can verify if a correction is required, possibly resulting in a full roll-back of the deployment

lines.text: And overnight? The load runs at four. If it does not finish, who finds out?
lines.plain: And overnight? The data load runs at 04:00. If it does not finish, who finds out?

lines.text: Alert before six. Today it pages me and I answer because it is my model. In February it pages a person who has never seen the model and the alert says load incomplete, which is useless.
lines.plain: There is an alert before 06:00. Today it calls me, and I answer, because the data model is mine. In February it will call somebody who has never seen the model, and the alert only says the load is incomplete, which is not useful.
ref: The goal is to identify potential issues before they become real problems and jeopardize the correct system deployment and operation

lines.text: Then that is a work item, not a promise. Rewrite the alert so it names the step and the last good batch, and it goes in the list tonight with Charles's name on it.
lines.plain: Then that is a work item, not a promise. Rewrite the alert so that it names the failed step and the last successful batch. It goes in the Work Items List tonight with Charles's name on it.
ref: Revisit the Deployment Plan as the project evolves and feedback from previous deployment efforts is gathered

lines.text: There is a worse one and it is not ours. The lending platform takes its maintenance window on the last Wednesday of the quarter. That is the twenty-sixth.
lines.plain: There is a bigger problem, and it is not ours. The lending platform has its maintenance window on the last Wednesday of each quarter. That is 26 September.

lines.text: Nobody says anything. Babbage puts both hands flat on the desk, which is what he does instead of swearing.
lines.plain: Nobody speaks. Babbage puts both hands flat on the desk. That is what he does instead of swearing.

lines.text: Then the four o'clock load reads a platform that is halfway through a patch, the replica gets yesterday's positions, and the smoke test fails correctly. Which is the worst kind of failure, because everything worked.
lines.plain: Then the 04:00 load reads a platform that is in the middle of being patched. The replica gets yesterday's positions. The smoke test then fails, and it fails correctly. That is the worst kind of failure, because every part worked as designed.

lines.text: The platform does not move for us. It is Lending Operations' system of record and it has its own release calendar and its own steering committee, and we are the dependency, not them.
lines.plain: The lending platform will not change its window for us. It is Lending Operations' official system, with its own release calendar and its own steering committee. We depend on it. It does not depend on us.
ref: Deployment and transition activities are also crucial to ensure that dependencies with other projects and/or information systems are taken into consideration

lines.text: Then we deploy on the twenty-fifth and hold. Two days dark instead of one. Ada, that is a change to your plan and I would like it written down rather than remembered by the four of us.
lines.plain: Then we deploy on 25 September and wait. The system stays switched off for two days instead of one. Ada, that is a change to your plan. I want it written down, not just remembered by the four of us.

lines.text: Revision five, tonight, and it goes to your duty manager before it goes to anyone else. She is the only reader who matters. If she cannot run it without ringing Charles, it is not a plan, it is a note.
lines.plain: It will be revision five, written tonight. It goes to your duty manager before anyone else. She is the only reader who matters. If she cannot follow it without telephoning Charles, then it is not a plan. It is a note.
ref: Contributes by bringing information related to operational processes and infrastructure, checking the feasibility, effectiveness and efficiency of the Deployment Plan and associated risks

lines.text: Last thing, and it is the one I actually came for. Eleven national authorities. Accounts, a first-line support route, and somebody who answers a telephone at seven in the morning in a language that is not Luxembourgish. Where is that in your plan?
lines.plain: One last point, and it is the reason I came. There are eleven national authorities. They need accounts, a support route for first contact, and somebody who answers the telephone at 07:00 in a language other than Luxembourgish. Where is that in your plan?

lines.text: It is not.
lines.plain: It is not in my plan.

lines.text: And it should not be. Ada's plan puts software on your infrastructure and proves it landed. Training eleven supervisors and standing up a support desk is the Transition Plan and the Business Implementation Plan, which is Grace's side of the house and which exists.
lines.plain: And it should not be. Ada's plan puts software onto your infrastructure and proves it arrived correctly. Training eleven supervisors and setting up a support desk belongs to the Transition Plan and the Business Implementation Plan. That is Grace's side of the organisation, and those documents exist.
g: Transition Plan
the PM2 document covering how the client organisation gets ready: training, support, communication
ref: The PM2 Transition Plan and Business Implementation Plan complement the Deployment Plan by covering the strategy to ensure that the client organisation is ready to use the system (training, support, etc.)

lines.text: Two documents, then. I would rather two documents with owners than one with none. Send me both and I will tell you which of my people is wrong about which.
lines.plain: Two documents, then. I prefer two documents with named owners to one document with no owner. Send me both and I will tell you which of my staff is wrong about which one.

lines.text: Gustave asked me in January why we were writing a deployment plan for a pipeline that deploys itself. I did not have an answer then. It is this room.
lines.plain: In January, Gustave asked me why we were writing a deployment plan when the pipeline deploys automatically. I had no answer then. The answer is this room.

lines.text: Sixteen forty. The dry-run ran twice, cleanly, and the second time the duty manager drove it and Babbage sat with his hands in his pockets, which was the point of the afternoon.
lines.plain: It is 16:40. The practice run was done twice, with no problems. The second time the duty manager ran it herself, and Babbage stood with his hands in his pockets. That was the purpose of the afternoon.

choice.prompt: Eleven national authorities need accounts, training and a support route before 27 September. Where does that work belong, and who writes it?
choice.promptPlain: Eleven national authorities need accounts, training and a support route before 27 September. Where does that work belong, and who writes it?

options.t: Not in the Deployment Plan. That plan stays technical — deploy, validate, monitor — written by Lovelace with the operations representative. Training and support go in the PM² Transition Plan and Business Implementation Plan.
options.tPlain: It does not go in the Deployment Plan. That plan stays technical: deploy, validate, monitor. Lovelace writes it with the operations representative. Training and support belong in the PM2 Transition Plan and Business Implementation Plan.

reply.text: Grace has had a Business Implementation Plan since November with eleven supervisors in it by name. Every few months somebody tries to fold it into a technical document, where nobody will read it.
reply.plain: Grace has had a Business Implementation Plan since November, with eleven supervisors named in it. Every few months somebody tries to merge it into a technical document, where nobody will read it.

options.why: The Deployment Plan defines the strategy, roles and tasks needed for IT operations to deploy, run and manage the system, and because it focuses on the technical aspects it lives next to cut-over, rollbacks and back-out procedures (p.82). The guide is explicit that the PM² Transition Plan and Business Implementation Plan complement it by covering the client organisation's readiness — training, support. Two artefacts, two owners, one release. The TeCo is Responsible for the Deployment Plan and the PM Accountable, with a representative of the operational unit contributing (p.83).
options.whyPlain: The Deployment Plan sets out the strategy, the roles and the tasks that let IT operations deploy, run and manage the system. Because it is technical, it sits beside cut-over, rollback and back-out procedures (page 82). The guide says clearly that the PM2 Transition Plan and Business Implementation Plan complete the picture by covering whether the client organisation is ready: training and support. Two documents, two owners, one release. The Team Coordinator is Responsible for the Deployment Plan and the Project Manager is Accountable, with someone from the operational unit contributing (page 83).
ref: Deployment Plan I A R S S S

options.t: Put it all in the Deployment Plan. One release, one document, one owner — operations should not have to read three files on the night.
options.tPlain: Put everything in the Deployment Plan. One release, one document, one owner. Operations should not have to read three files on the night.

reply.text: Then my duty manager opens a fifty-page file at half past nine looking for the configuration order and reads six pages about a training course in Riga. She will stop reading. They always stop reading.
reply.plain: Then my duty manager opens a fifty-page file at 21:30, looking for the order of configuration steps, and finds six pages about a training course in Riga. She will stop reading. People always stop reading.

options.why: The Deployment Plan must have enough detail to allow the IT operations team to deploy, run and manage the system, and its three prescribed sections are Deployment in Production, Validate the Solution, and Monitor, Report and Respond to problems (p.82). Nothing in those three sections is about people's readiness. Merging the two does not create one owner; it hides the business-readiness work inside a document owned by a technical role who cannot deliver it, on a night when nobody has time to read it.
options.whyPlain: The Deployment Plan must contain enough detail for the IT operations team to deploy, run and manage the system. Its three required sections are Deployment in Production, Validate the Solution, and Monitor, Report and Respond to problems (page 82). None of those sections is about whether people are ready. Merging the two documents does not create a single owner. It hides the business readiness work inside a technical document, owned by someone who cannot deliver it, and read on a night when nobody has time.
ref: The Deployment Plan should include the following sections

options.t: Hand the whole Deployment Plan to Leonardo's operations team to write. They run production, they carry the pager, and they know their own infrastructure better than the Team Coordinator does.
options.tPlain: Give the whole Deployment Plan to Leonardo's operations team to write. They run production, they carry the pager, and they know their own infrastructure better than the Team Coordinator does.

reply.text: They know the infrastructure. They do not know that the gateway ships dark, or which of four units can be reversed in ninety seconds, or why the smoke test picks the member state at random. Those are three weeks of our arguments.
reply.plain: They know the infrastructure. They do not know that the gateway is installed switched off, or which of the four units can be reversed in ninety seconds, or why the smoke test chooses the member state at random. Those points come from three weeks of our discussions.

options.why: The RAM gives the Team Coordinator Responsible and the Project Manager Accountable, with the Agile Team Members, Architecture Owner and Product Owner supporting; the operational unit representative contributes but does not own it (p.82–83). The reason is alignment: the TeCo writes it against the Development Work Plan's release schedule and against the project-level Transition Plan. Where the organisation is siloed with an independent IT Operations department, the guide's answer is that operations must be integrally involved — involved, not handed the pen.
options.whyPlain: In the responsibility table, the Team Coordinator is Responsible and the Project Manager is Accountable. The team members, Architecture Owner and Product Owner support. The operations representative contributes but does not own the plan (pages 82 and 83). The reason is alignment: the Team Coordinator writes it against the release schedule in the Development Work Plan and against the project's Transition Plan. Where operations is a separate department, the guide says operations must be fully involved. Involved is not the same as being given the pen.
ref: Responsible for creating the Deployment Plan aligned with the Development Work Plan (Release Schedule) and with the project-level Transition Plan

options.t: Drop the separate plan. The continuous delivery pipeline is the deployment plan — it is defined in code, it is in the Development Handbook, and a document will only go stale.
options.tPlain: Do not keep a separate plan. The continuous delivery pipeline is the deployment plan. It is defined in code, it is described in the Development Handbook, and a document will only become out of date.

reply.text: The pipeline has never once decided at twenty-two hundred whether to put ninety minutes of data back. It cannot. That decision has a person's name on it and the name is not in any repository.
reply.plain: The pipeline has never had to decide, at 22:00, whether to spend ninety minutes restoring the data. It cannot make that decision. That decision has a person's name attached to it, and that name is not stored in any repository.

options.why: The guide treats the pipeline as a strategic decision that must itself be described and validated in the Deployment Plan — the pipeline is content of the plan, not a substitute for it (p.83). The plan carries what no pipeline holds: the back-out decision and its owner, the validation criteria, the monitoring and escalation route, and the operational unit's confirmation that it can run the thing. It is also a living artefact, revisited as feedback from previous deployments arrives — which is precisely why revision five exists.
options.whyPlain: The guide treats the pipeline as a strategic decision that must be described and validated inside the Deployment Plan. The pipeline is part of the plan's content, not a replacement for it (page 83). The plan holds what no pipeline holds: the back-out decision and who takes it, the validation criteria, the monitoring and escalation route, and the operations team's confirmation that they can run it. It is also a living document, updated as feedback from earlier deployments arrives. That is exactly why revision five exists.
ref: The setup of a Continuous Delivery Pipeline is a strategic decision that must be described and validated in the plan

lovelace.f: Afraid the plan reads as a note and gets improvised at twenty-two hundred.

leonardo.o: Solution Provider, Head of IT & Digital. Supplies the operational unit representative.
leonardo.k: Knows his duty manager owns this at three in the morning from the first of February.
leonardo.w: Wants a plan his own people can execute without telephoning the project team.
leonardo.f: Afraid of deploying something at midnight that turns out to be a policy decision.

einstein.o: Architecture Owner. Supports the deployment approach; named the platform dependency.
einstein.k: Knows the gateway can deploy dark, separating what ships from what opens.
einstein.w: Wants deployment and opening treated as two events with two different owners.
einstein.f: Afraid a dependency nobody owns is discovered on the night of a cut-over.

babbage.o: Agile Team Member, data engineer. Supports with the load, the alert and the smoke test.
babbage.k: Knows the replica reload is ninety minutes and cannot be made faster by wanting it.
babbage.w: Wants the alert to name the step and the last good batch before he stops answering it.
babbage.f: Afraid he is still the escalation path in March because nobody replaced him.

note: Guide check: section 7.2.4, pp.82-83, with the Deployment & Transition theme at section 4.14, p.40. The Deployment Plan defines the strategy, roles and responsibilities and tasks needed so the information system can be deployed, run and managed by the IT operations team; because it focuses on the technical aspects it sits close to cut-over, rollbacks and back-out procedures for contingency and risk management. It has three prescribed sections: Deployment in Production, Validate the Solution, and Monitor, Report and Respond to problems. It must carry enough detail for operations to work from, and it pairs with the Operational Model. The PM² Transition Plan and Business Implementation Plan complement it by covering the client organisation's readiness — training, support. Guidelines: compatible with the Development Handbook, with the continuous delivery pipeline itself described and validated in the plan; DevSecOps, or integral involvement of IT Operations where the organisation is siloed; a living artefact revisited as deployment feedback arrives; aligned with the Release Plan; and tested first, with the operations team deploying it in pre-production. RASCI p.83: BM I, PM A, TeCo R, PrOw S, ArOw S, ATeM S, plus a representative of the relevant operational unit contributing. The theme at p.40 adds that deployment and transition activities must account for dependencies with other projects and information systems. Pages 40, 82-83.
notePlain: Rule: the Deployment Plan sets out the strategy, the roles and responsibilities, and the tasks needed so the IT operations team can deploy, run and manage the system (page 82). It is a technical document, so it deals with cut-over, rollbacks and back-out procedures. It has three required sections: Deployment in Production, Validate the Solution, and Monitor, Report and Respond to problems. It must be detailed enough for operations to use, and it works together with the Operational Model. The PM2 Transition Plan and Business Implementation Plan complete it by covering whether the client organisation is ready, which means training and support (page 82). The guidelines say: it must fit the Development Handbook, and the continuous delivery pipeline must itself be described and checked in the plan; IT operations must be fully involved when they are a separate department; the plan is a living document, updated as feedback from earlier deployments arrives; it must line up with the Release Plan; and it must be tested first, with operations deploying it in a pre-production environment (page 83). Who is who: the Team Coordinator is Responsible, the Project Manager is Accountable, the Business Manager is Informed, and a representative of the operations unit contributes (page 83). The theme on page 40 adds that deployment and transition work must take account of dependencies on other projects and systems. Pages 40, 82 and 83.

title: Nine of eleven
where: ESM, Kirchberg — the long room, fourth floor

lines.text: One week to the twenty-seventh. On the wall, three iterations laid end to end: sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, ninety-one points accepted between them, and a release that is the sum of all three and the output of none.
lines.plain: There is one week left before 27 September. On the wall are three iterations side by side: 16, 17 and 18. Together they delivered 91 accepted points. The release is the total of all three. It is not the output of any single one.
ref: A Release is the result of the incremental process applied throughout several iterations, as the team releases the solution as a viable product (or a Minimum Viable Product) that is ready to be used by the stakeholders
g: Minimum Viable Product
the smallest version of a solution that is genuinely usable by stakeholders

lines.text: The overlay was accepted on the thirty-first of August. The gateway was accepted last Friday. Everything in Release 3 has been demonstrated, accepted and deployed, and none of it is a release yet.
lines.plain: The scenario overlay was accepted on 31 August. The external gateway was accepted last Friday. Everything in Release 3 has been demonstrated, accepted and installed. None of it is a release yet.

lines.text: Because it is dark. Two-six-three has been in production since Tuesday of last week with the switch down and eleven supervisors who cannot tell it exists.
lines.plain: That is because it is switched off. Work item 263 has been in production since Tuesday of last week, with the switch off. The eleven national supervisors cannot tell that it exists.
g: feature flag
a switch in the code that hides finished work until somebody turns it on

lines.text: Which is the only reason this meeting is calm. The release is the twenty-seventh because that is the day I say a supervisor may look at it. Not the day it shipped.
lines.plain: That is the only reason this meeting is calm. The release date is 27 September because that is the day I say a supervisor may look at it. It is not the day the code was installed.

lines.text: Then say it in my language. On the twenty-seventh, personal data held by this institution becomes readable by a public authority in another member state. What permits that, in writing, signed, per authority?
lines.plain: Then say it in my terms. On 27 September, personal data held by this institution becomes readable by a public authority in another member state. What permits that? I want it in writing, signed, for each authority.

lines.text: An administrative arrangement each. Eleven drafted in June, nine signed, two not. Estonia is with their legal service and Cyprus has asked for a change to clause four.
lines.plain: Each authority signs an administrative arrangement. Eleven were drafted in June. Nine are signed and two are not. Estonia's is with their legal service, and Cyprus has asked for a change to clause four.
g: legal basis
the written legal ground that allows personal data to be shared with someone

lines.text: Then nine.
lines.plain: Then nine authorities, not eleven.

lines.text: Louis, the code is identical. It costs nothing to open eleven and it costs me a paragraph to explain nine.
lines.plain: Louis, the software is the same for all of them. Opening it to eleven costs nothing. Explaining nine costs me a paragraph.

lines.text: It costs nothing until March, when somebody asks on what basis Tallinn read a Lithuanian position, and the honest answer is that the switch was one switch. Nine.
lines.plain: It costs nothing until March. Then somebody asks on what basis Tallinn read a Lithuanian position, and the honest answer is that there was only one switch. Nine.

lines.text: The switch is per authority. It has been per authority since the fifth, because Alan made it a condition in refinement and Hedy built it in a day and a half.
lines.plain: The switch works separately for each authority. It has done since 5 September, because Alan required it during refinement and Hedy built it in a day and a half.

lines.text: I made it a condition because a single switch is a single mistake. And before anyone turns any of the nine on, I want the row filter proved by somebody who did not write it.
lines.plain: I required it because one switch means one possible mistake. And before anyone turns on any of the nine, I want the row-level filter tested by somebody who did not build it.

lines.text: And before you say it, I know. Line four of the Definition of Done says the team tested it. I am asking for a different thing, once, for this release only, because this release is the first one where being wrong is not an internal matter.
lines.plain: And before you say it, I know. Line four of the Definition of Done says the team tested it. I am asking for something different, once, for this release only. This is the first release where a mistake would not stay inside the institution.
ref: Depending on the solution being built, additional levels of formalism and validation may be required

lines.text: Security Assurance ran it Monday and Tuesday. Four hundred and twelve queries as a Lithuanian account, none of them mine, none of them Hedy's. Two got more than Lithuania.
lines.plain: The Security Assurance team ran the test on Monday and Tuesday. They made 412 queries using a Lithuanian account. Nobody from our team was involved. Two of those queries returned more than Lithuania.
ref: some organisations require projects' software to be validated by a quality assurance team, working in parallel with the Agile Project Core Team (A-PCT)

lines.text: Hopper stops writing. Brandeis does not look surprised, which is worse than looking surprised.
lines.plain: Hopper stops writing. Brandeis does not look surprised, which is worse than if he did.

lines.text: Both in the maturity aggregate. Buckets over ten years pooled across the whole book before the filter ran, so the total leaked the shape of Portugal. Fixed Wednesday, retested Thursday morning, four hundred and twelve clean.
lines.plain: Both problems were in the maturity totals. Buckets over ten years were combined across the whole portfolio before the filter was applied, so the total revealed the shape of Portugal's position. It was fixed on Wednesday, retested on Thursday morning, and all 412 queries were then clean.

lines.text: That is the finding I would have written in October. I would rather have it on a Wednesday. And the amendment record?
lines.plain: That is exactly the finding I would have written in October. I prefer to have it on a Wednesday. And what about the amendment record?

lines.text: External readers see a role and a date. Loan Operations Officer, eleventh of March. Internal readers see the staff identifier, as before. Two views of one record, and the screening signed on the sixth.
lines.plain: External readers see a role and a date: Loan Operations Officer, 11 March. Internal readers still see the staff identifier, as before. There are two views of one record. The data protection screening was signed on 6 September.

lines.text: In December of last year I said the feed goes one way and there is no path back into the platform, and that I would quote it at you in 2030. I am early. Nothing on the gateway writes.
lines.plain: In December last year I said that the data feed goes only one way, with no path back into the lending platform, and that I would repeat it to you in 2030. I am early. Nothing on the gateway can write data.

lines.text: So on the twenty-seventh I have nine authorities, a scenario overlay Risk has wanted since April, and two member states I have to telephone myself.
lines.plain: So on 27 September I have nine authorities, a scenario overlay that Risk has wanted since April, and two member states that I must telephone myself.

lines.text: Release 3 is delivered on the twenty-seventh. The benefit for two of the eleven is not. Those are different sentences, Grace, and if you merge them upstairs you will be explaining it again in November.
lines.plain: Release 3 is delivered on 27 September. The benefit for two of the eleven authorities is not delivered. Those are two different statements. If you combine them upstairs, Grace, you will have to explain it again in November.

lines.text: There is training in this too, and it is not code. Eleven half-days, nine of them now, and support cover from seven. That is not iteration 18's work, so I am splitting the team.
lines.plain: There is also training, and that is not software work. Eleven half-day sessions, nine of them now, plus support cover from 07:00. That is not the work of iteration 18, so I am splitting the team.
ref: the process of releasing may require some additional preparation and some extra activities (training users, fixing a critical bug, etc.)

lines.text: Gustave and Charles on release work to the twenty-seventh. Hedy and Albert stay on the builder, because December does not move for September. Two halves of one team, one plan, one stand-up.
lines.plain: Gustave and Charles work on the release until 27 September. Hedy and Albert continue on the self-service builder, because the December date does not move for September. Two halves of one team, one plan, one stand-up meeting.
ref: An Agile team may also be split into two sub-teams that work together in parallel

lines.text: And in January the whole team does that work and nothing else. That iteration is planned like every other one — goal, list, review, retrospective — it just contains no new features.
lines.plain: And in January the whole team does that kind of work and nothing else. That iteration is planned like any other one, with a goal, a list, a review and a retrospective. It simply contains no new features.
g: Transition Iteration
an iteration spent preparing a release for use instead of building new features
ref: It remains an iteration and as such, it should be carried out just like a regular one (proper ceremonies, Iteration Planning with a Work Items List, etc.)

lines.text: Send me the two arrangements when they come back. And do not open Estonia because it is Friday and the switch is right there.
lines.plain: Send me the two arrangements when they are signed. And do not open Estonia just because it is Friday and the switch is easy to reach.

lines.text: Nobody touches the switch but me, and I do it at nine on the twenty-seventh with Alan in the room. Nine authorities. I will write the two names on the board so we all have to look at them.
lines.plain: Nobody touches the switch except me. I will do it at 09:00 on 27 September, with Alan present. Nine authorities. I will write the two missing names on the board so that we all have to look at them.

note: Guide check: section 3.3.3, pp.21-22, with the independent tester at p.64. A Release is the result of the incremental process applied across several iterations: the team releases the solution as a viable product, or a Minimum Viable Product, ready to be used by the stakeholders. By default the continuous exposure of work items plus demonstrated and validated iteration results already enables a solid release, but depending on the solution additional levels of formalism and validation may be required, and specific requirements may demand extra validation steps to confirm the release is fully compliant with the agreed Definition of Done. Complex releases may need extra preparation and activities — training users, fixing a critical bug, extra functional, performance, load, system and integration testing, documenting the system, training support personnel, updating the Development or Deployment Plan — which can be planned as a Transition Iteration. A Transition Iteration is still an iteration: proper ceremonies, Iteration Planning, a Work Items List. The team may decide no new features are developed in it, and an agile team may be split into two sub-teams working in parallel, one on release activities and one on the follow-on release. One Transition Iteration may not be enough. Page 64 allows an independent quality assurance team working in parallel with the A-PCT where the organisation requires it. Pages 21-22, 64.
notePlain: Rule: a release is the result of the step-by-step work of several iterations. The team gives the stakeholders a usable product, or a minimum usable product, that is ready to be used (page 21). Normally the constant showing of work items and the accepted iteration results are enough to make a solid release. But depending on what is being built, more formality and more checking may be needed, and some requirements need extra validation steps to prove the release fully meets the agreed Definition of Done (page 22). A complex release may need extra preparation: training users, fixing a serious defect, extra performance, load, system and integration testing, writing documentation, training support staff, and updating the Development or Deployment Plan. This work can be planned as a Transition Iteration. A Transition Iteration is still a normal iteration, with the usual ceremonies, an Iteration Planning session and a Work Items List. The team may decide to build no new features in it. The team may also split into two groups working at the same time, one on release work and one on the next release. One Transition Iteration may not be enough (page 22). Page 64 allows an independent quality team to check the software in parallel with the team where the organisation requires it. note: Guide check: sections 7.3.2 and 7.3.3, pp.85-86. To enable overall monitoring of project performance during Executing, the Agile Project Core Team documents and manages domain-specific risks, issues, decisions and changes; managing them lets the Project Core Team identify items that affect overall project performance and must be handled by the general project organisation, supports the Project Manager's reporting and forecasting, and gives the PM the coordination tool for assigning items back to the team. The PM² management plans and artefacts are the starting point: Risks to the Risk Management Plan and Risk Log; Issues to the Issues Management Plan and Issue Log; Decisions to the Decision Log; Changes to the Project Change Management Plan, Change Log and Change Request Form; plus a Testing Log referenced to the Test Plans and Deliverables Acceptance Plan, and a Retrospectives Log referenced to the Project-End Report. On reporting: the development aspect contributes domain-specific status and progress to the project's reports, the Project Status Report carries the Development Status Report to the Managing Layer, and for PM²-Agile projects the Project Progress Report is frequent — bi-monthly or quarterly rather than yearly — so significant scope changes are captured and managed. It contains a Project Overview and Project Details, and ad hoc status reporting with an updated Project Charter may be needed depending on scope impact. Pages 85-86, with the logs guideline at p.84.
notePlain: Rule: during Executing, the agile team writes down and manages its own risks, issues, decisions and changes. Doing this lets the Project Core Team spot items that affect the whole project and must be handled by the wider project organisation. It also supports the Project Manager's reporting and forecasting, and it gives the Project Manager a way to assign items back to the team (page 85). The PM2 management plans and documents are the starting point. Risks go with the Risk Management Plan and Risk Log. Issues go with the Issues Management Plan and Issue Log. Decisions go in the Decision Log. Changes go with the Project Change Management Plan, the Change Log and the Change Request Form. Two more logs are added: a Testing Log, linked to the Test Plans and the Deliverables Acceptance Plan, and a Retrospectives Log, linked to the Project-End Report (page 85). For reporting, the development side feeds its status into the project reports. The Project Status Report carries the Development Status Report upward. For agile projects the Project Progress Report is written often, every two or three months instead of once a year, so that big scope changes are caught in time. It has an overview section and a details section, and an extra report with an updated Project Charter may be needed if the scope moves a lot (pages 85 and 86). Pages 84 to 86.

note: Guide check: section 6.5, pp.64-65, with the Team Coordinator's responsibilities at p.62. Introducing PM²-Agile changes the governance model's roles to support decentralised decision-making, self-organising teams, permanent business involvement and relentless improvement; the new roles take on some responsibilities usually assigned to the Project Manager, but the PM role is not removed. Methodology compliance becomes shared: the PM educates the team on PM² per the Project Handbook, the TeCo guarantees agile values per the Development Handbook, and the TeCo facilitates the ceremonies while the PM participates as a regular Agile Team Member. Team and progress management passes to the self-organising A-PCT, which frees the PM to focus on the problems and impediments the team raises via the TeCo. Managing business stakeholders' expectations passes to the Product Owner as permanent point of contact; the PM and BM intervene only when expectations are not aligned or the PrOw and the team cannot reach consensus. For the Business Manager, PM²-Agile clearly extends the range of action: she coordinates client-side activities and roles, the PrOw becomes the liaison between User Representatives and the provider, and the BM must empower the PrOw for day-to-day decisions and keep her aligned with the BM and the BIG — an empowered, aligned PrOw is what allows the real benefits of PM²-Agile to surface. The TeCo is responsible for reporting work progress to the PM (p.62). Pages 62, 64-65, with the reporting RAM at p.84.
notePlain: Rule: bringing in PM2-Agile changes the roles in the governance model, to support decisions taken lower down, teams that organise themselves, business people involved all the time, and constant improvement. The new roles take over some tasks that usually belong to the Project Manager, but the Project Manager role is not removed (page 64). Method compliance becomes shared: the Project Manager teaches PM2 from the Project Handbook, and the Team Coordinator guarantees agile values from the Development Handbook. The Team Coordinator facilitates the ceremonies while the Project Manager takes part as an ordinary team member (page 65). Managing the team's work passes to the team itself, which frees the Project Manager to work on the obstacles the team raises through the Team Coordinator (page 65). Managing business expectations passes to the Product Owner, who becomes the permanent contact point between the two organisations. The Project Manager and Business Manager step in only when expectations do not match, or when the Product Owner and the team cannot agree (page 65). For the Business Manager, PM2-Agile clearly widens the range of action. She coordinates the client side, the Product Owner becomes the link between user representatives and the provider, and the Business Manager must give the Product Owner power to decide day to day and keep her aligned with the business strategy. A Product Owner who is empowered and aligned is what lets the real benefits of PM2-Agile appear (page 65). The Team Coordinator reports work progress to the Project Manager (page 62). Pages 62, 64, 65 and 84.

Projects pass through four distinct PM² phases, and although planning characteristics may be less tangible at the level of the agile team, the phases still exist and a common understanding of them should be fostered; the overall sequential character follows the concept that a project has a defined beginning and ending date, so activities start with initiating and planning, lead to implementation, and end with acceptance, transitioning and closing. As the project nears completion the focus shifts to ensuring the solution is well integrated into the overall project deliverables and contributes to the accrual of the benefits desired by the organisation, with a specific emphasis on ensuring the organisation can assume ownership and be accountable for the evolution and maintenance of the information system when the project closes. Value is measured with a measuring and learning framework. At p.61 the Project Owner is the key project decision maker and accountable for project success, while the Solution Provider assumes overall accountability for the project deliverables. The artefact lifecycle rows are the structural argument against a post-closure project: Deployment Plan created in Planning and updated in Executing, nothing in Closing; Development Status Report created in Planning and Executing, nothing in Closing. Pages 17-18, 61, 83, 85.
notePlain: Rule: projects pass through four PM2 phases. Even though planning is less visible at the agile team's level, the phases still exist, and everyone should share the same understanding of them (page 17). A project has a fixed start and end date, so the work starts with initiating and planning, leads to building, and ends with acceptance, transition and closing (page 17). As the project nears the end, attention moves to making sure the solution fits into the whole set of deliverables and helps produce the benefits the organisation wants. The guide adds a specific point: make sure the organisation can take ownership and be accountable for future changes and upkeep of the system when the project closes (page 18). The value delivered is measured with a measuring and learning framework (page 18). On page 61, the Project Owner is the main decision maker and is accountable for the project's success, and the Solution Provider is accountable for the deliverables. The artefact tables make the same point in another way: the Deployment Plan is created in Planning and updated in Executing, with nothing in Closing; the Development Status Report is created in Planning and Executing, with nothing in Closing (pages 83 and 85). Pages 17, 18, 61, 83 and 85.

note: Guide check: section 5.5, p.57, with section 2.3, p.8, and the mindsets at pp.22-23. Retrospecting is not new in PM²: the Project-End Review meeting captures lessons learned and post-project recommendations so teams benefit from the experience acquired, and PM² already asks that improvement opportunities be captured throughout the project rather than only at the end, where most may already have been forgotten. PM²-Agile takes retrospection further in two ways: the Iteration Retrospective happens at the end of every iteration, giving a permanent and recurrent evaluation of the team's performance made by the team itself; and the team does not wait until the end of the project to adjust, integrating improvement opportunities into its work as soon as possible. The retrospective is focused on real problems affecting the team, and finds solutions the team can implement without waiting for management approval. At the end of the project, when Lessons Learned are collected, the repository where the team keeps its Iteration Retrospective logs is an invaluable source that enriches the lessons learned and the post-project recommendations — an input to them, not a replacement. Section 2.3 states the same relation directly: the Lessons Learned captured at the end of a project remain valuable, and the habit of frequent reviewing and retrospecting is infused across the project continuum in addition. The mindsets make sharing knowledge and actively managing lessons learned an obligation to the wider organisation. Pages 8, 22-23, 57, with the log reference at p.85.
notePlain: Rule: looking back is not new in PM2. The Project-End Review meeting collects lessons learned and recommendations for after the project, so that teams gain from the experience. PM2 already asks that improvement ideas be collected during the project, not only at the end, when most of them have been forgotten (page 57). PM2-Agile goes further in two ways. First, the Iteration Retrospective happens at the end of every iteration, which gives a constant, repeated review of the team's performance, made by the team itself. Second, the team does not wait until the end of the project to change things; improvements go into its work as soon as possible (page 57). The retrospective deals with real problems that affect the team, and finds solutions the team can apply without waiting for management approval. At the end of the project, when Lessons Learned are collected, the store of retrospective logs is a very valuable source that enriches the lessons learned and the recommendations. It is an input to them, not a replacement for them (page 57). Page 8 says the same thing directly: lessons learned at the end of a project stay valuable, and the habit of frequent review is added across the whole project. The mindsets make sharing knowledge and actively managing lessons learned a duty to the wider organisation (page 22). Pages 8, 22, 23, 57 and 85.

note: Guide check: section 3.4, pp.22-23, with section 3.3.1, p.18. The PM² Mindsets ask project teams to maintain an outcomes orientation across all project management activities, to involve project stakeholders in the organisational change needed to maximise project benefits, and to share knowledge and actively manage lessons learned. The Infrequently Asked Questions that keep the mindsets live include 'Have we improved?' and 'Is there life after the project?' — the second of which is the closing question of any project, and the one POLLUX answers with a service backlog rather than a report. The PM²-Agile drivers add that there is no such thing as an Agile project, only PM²-Agile projects, and that teams should concentrate on the flow of value, where the customer defines value. Page 18 states the delivery consequence: the iterative and incremental nature of PM²-Agile creates a sustainable and paced delivery of value to the organisation, measured rigorously using a measuring and learning framework, and as the project nears completion the emphasis falls on the organisation assuming ownership and accountability for evolution and maintenance. POLLUX closes with three of five success criteria demonstrable on the day; SC1 waits for the April quarter-end pack and SC5 for an audit follow-up in September, both owned by the Project Owner and the Business Manager against the Business Case. Pages 18, 22-23.
notePlain: Rule: the PM2 Mindsets ask project teams to stay focused on outcomes in everything they do, to involve stakeholders in the organisational change needed to get the most benefit, and to share knowledge and actively manage lessons learned (page 22). The questions that keep those mindsets alive include 'Have we improved?' and 'Is there life after the project?' (page 23). The second is the closing question of any project, and POLLUX answers it with a service backlog instead of a report. The PM2-Agile drivers add that there is no such thing as an agile project, only PM2-Agile projects, and that teams should focus on the flow of value, where the customer decides what value is (page 23). Page 18 gives the delivery result: the step-by-step nature of PM2-Agile creates a steady, sustainable delivery of value to the organisation, measured properly with a measuring and learning framework. And as the project nears its end, the emphasis falls on the organisation taking ownership and accountability for future changes and upkeep. POLLUX closes with three of its five success criteria provable on the day. SC1 waits for the April quarter-end pack and SC5 for an audit review in September. Both belong to the Project Owner and the Business Manager, measured against the Business Case. Pages 18, 22 and 23.
